blocks.md: Along the **East African coast**, from Somalia to Mozambique, lived the **Swahili** people in trading **city-states** such as **Mombasa**, **Kilwa** and Zanzibar. Their language, **Kiswahili**, is an African (Bantu) language with many borrowed Arabic words. They traded across the **Indian Ocean** with Arabia, Persia, India and China, using sailing boats (dhows) and the **monsoon winds**, which blow one way for part of the year and the other way for the rest.

blocks.alt: Four boxes showing gold from Zimbabwe going through Swahili ports to Arabia and India and goods returning.

blocks.title: Swahili trade
blocks.md: Swahili ports **exported** gold, ivory, timber, iron and slaves and **imported** cloth, beads, glass, porcelain and spices. The merchants built houses, mosques and palaces of coral stone. Most Swahili towns were ruled by their own sultans or elders and did not form a single empire.

blocks.title: Great Zimbabwe
blocks.md: **Great Zimbabwe** (in the present country of Zimbabwe) was a large stone-walled town of the Shona-speaking peoples, flourishing around the 11th–15th centuries. Its stone walls and towers were built without mortar. It was rich in **cattle**, **gold** and ivory, which were traded with the coast and then across the ocean. Its name means 'stone houses'.

The towns of the coast and the interior were linked by trade: gold from the Zimbabwe plateau reached Kilwa and other ports, and was sent to Arabia and beyond. Objects such as Chinese porcelain and glass beads have been found at Great Zimbabwe, which shows these long-distance links. The **Kingdom of Aksum** (in present-day Ethiopia) earlier traded with Egypt, Arabia and India and became a Christian kingdom in the 4th century.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- The Swahili coast was not one country or empire; it was many independent city-states.
- Great Zimbabwe was built by Africans, as archaeological evidence shows.
- Monsoon winds are seasonal winds; they are not the same as the harmattan of West Africa.

blocks.title: Example 1: monsoon trade
blocks.statement: Why were monsoon winds important to the Swahili traders?
steps: The winds blow towards India for part of the year.
They blow back to Africa later in the year.
Sailors could plan return voyages with the winds.
blocks.answer: They allowed regular voyages across the Indian Ocean.

blocks.title: Example 2: Great Zimbabwe
blocks.statement: Give two reasons why Great Zimbabwe became important.
steps: It controlled valuable cattle and gold.
It was connected to the coast by trade.
So it became rich and powerful.
